cover.hook: Anthropic's IPO filing: its own models could be used in cyberattacks.
cover.sub: Its S-1 names foreign governments and criminal groups, and says its safeguards may not prove adequate.

slides.title: Who it's worried about
slides.body: Anthropic expects bad actors, including foreign governments, to step up efforts to access its newest frontier models as their cyber capabilities improve, per CyberScoop's reading of the S-1.

slides.title: Agents widen the attack surface
slides.body: The filing says AI agents create 'distinct' attack surfaces: their links to tools, databases, APIs and third-party systems can be compromised or manipulated to feed the agent malicious instructions.

slides.label: models under US export controls

slides.title: Hard to insure, hard to report
slides.body: Anthropic says it may struggle to insure some incidents tied to its models, and EU breach-reporting deadlines could be hard to meet. It also cites an FTC civil investigative demand from October.

slides.title: If you run AI agents
items: List every tool and API each agent can call
Treat tool output as untrusted input
Ask AI vendors how they report incidents

items.send_to: whoever approves your AI dev tools

cover.hook: Warp: about 1% of users may have had AI agent logs exposed.
cover.sub: The agentic dev environment says a vendor in its infrastructure was exploited. It caught it within hours.

slides.title: What happened
slides.body: Warp says agent decision logs and telemetry were exposed in an attack on a third-party vendor in its infrastructure. CEO Zach Lloyd calls it 'active and narrow-banded'. Warp learned of it on a Friday.

slides.label: of Warp users may be affected
slides.note: Warp's website says it has at least 800,000 users

slides.title: Still unknown
slides.body: Warp hasn't named the vendor or the flaw, or said whether source code, prompts or credentials were in the data. An analysis cited by BleepingComputer suggests an 'agent swarm' ran the attack.

slides.title: The response
slides.body: Warp notified affected users, brought in CrowdStrike and told law enforcement. It follows a separate OpenCode incident where stored API keys of about 1.4% of users were exposed.

slides.title: For teams using AI dev tools
items: Assume agent traces can hold secrets
Set short retention for agent logs
Rotate keys pasted into agent sessions
Expect phishing that cites the breach

items.x_text:
testmetest npm worm (Miasma family): JFrog found 42 real GitHub repos from 11 owners armed. It hooks AI coding tools and plants a wiper that deletes your home folder if the stolen GitHub token is revoked. Isolate before you revoke.

#SupplyChain #InfoSec
items.ig_caption:
Revoke the stolen token, and it wipes your home folder. 🪱

What researchers found (via The Register, 26 Oct):
→ The 'testmetest' npm worm, part of the Miasma family, spread through 18 npm packages
→ JFrog found 42 real GitHub repositories from 11 owners already armed, with account hijacks going back to July
→ 12.9–13.7 MB payload blobs are big enough to evade the GitHub search and API paths used to find this kind of compromise
→ Execution hooks target AI coding tools and dev tools, including Claude, Gemini, Cursor and VS Code
→ It steals credentials and installs a wiper that deletes the home directory when the stolen GitHub token is revoked

What to do: if a dev machine is hit, isolate it and remove the token monitor before revoking, then rotate every secret it could reach. Set ignore-scripts in npm and review unexpected .claude or .vscode files in repos.
